title: My Confusion with Inclusion
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien, who coordinates student-support funding in an Australian school, describes a bizarre conflict between what government facilitators reward in disability inclusion funding meetings and what educational research supports. He lists practices the funding process rates highly that are not best practice, including learning-styles language, an array of fidget toys, laptops in place of developing handwriting, reliance on font choices, extensive one-to-one support, and even ordinary explicit teaching rated as a substantial adjustment. Using David Didau, Daniel Willingham and Jared Cooney Horvath as touchstones, he argues that one-to-one support and device substitution can hinder the learning of the students they are meant to help. His stance is pragmatic: tell facilitators what they want to hear to secure funding, then advise teachers on what actually works. He attributes the mismatch partly to a roughly six-year lag between research and implementation.
points: Funding processes reward visible, differentiated adjustments such as devices and fidget buffets over the evidence-based practice of strong tier 1 instruction.
Replacing handwriting with a laptop may never address the root deficit, much as suggesting a bike to a slow runner does not improve running.
Heavy teaching-assistant support can leave students helped to complete tasks but not to learn, so support staff need training to give scaffolds, not answers.
Explicit teaching, with chunking, checking and worked examples, was treated as a substantial adjustment even though it is what every student should get.
Brien admits to code switching between funding language and practice, and the research-to-practice lag explains why the criteria trail best practice.
quotes: It is less about what will actually support the students learning and more about telling the facilitators what they are trained to want to hear. It is a bizarre conflict that means to best support our students we need to actively document for inferior adjustments and then inform teachers what they should be doing to best support the students in practice.
Yes, we have here a learning styles reference in 2026. It took every bit of willpower I have to keep my mouth closed.
Imagine telling an aspiring runner that it currently takes them a long time to run 5k so maybe they should just use a bike. The facilitators though, love this.

The irony here is that providing a student with 1:1 support is considered a substantial or extensive adjustment when in reality it is likely that too much support is going to hinder their potential learning growth. Yes, 1:1 support is definitely required when students have high level needs, however education support staff need significant professional learning to ensure that they are providing scaffolds, not answers.

The facilitator loved this and gave us a “substantial” rating in multiple categories despite it being the exact way we expect our teachers to teach to every single student in the room. Most students with additional needs do not just need great tier 1 instruction, they need more of it.

This was really a situation where we just had to agree and move on because although we could correct them, we could then jeopardise potential funding to support that student which would defeat the purpose of the whole operation.

I’ve been told that the gap between research and implementation is around 6 years in education, so it makes sense that sometimes the goal posts for these funding requests lag behind best practice. It becomes such a strange exercise in code switching to bounce between two competing mindsets of what works best for students with additional needs and the needs for additional funding.
